Task 1: Introduction, History, Pipelines & Tokenizer¶

  • Objective: Explore the history and trade-offs of Transformer models while inspecting how Hugging Face pipelines, tokenizers, and pretrained encoder architectures process text under the hood.
  • Expected Output: Sentiment predictions on 5 test sentences, historical timeline and impact/disadvantage summaries, sub-word tokenisation breakdowns, padded batch tensors, and a complete configuration and parameter summary of DistilBERT.

What happens inside a pipeline() call? A single call to clf(sentences) hides three distinct stages:

  1. Tokenisation: Raw text strings are split into sub-word tokens, mapped to integer vocabulary IDs (input_ids), wrapped with special boundary tokens, and paired with an attention_mask.
  2. Model Forward Pass: The integer tensors are fed through the pretrained Transformer layers (model.eval() mode) to compute raw, unnormalised prediction scores called logits.
  3. Post-Processing: A Softmax function converts the logits into probabilities summing to 1, and the highest-scoring index is mapped back to a human-readable string label (POSITIVE or NEGATIVE).

1.2 Timeline of the Transformer Revolution¶

Year Model / Paper Why It Mattered
2014–2015 Seq2Seq with Attention (Bahdanau et al. / Luong et al.) Allowed RNN decoders to dynamically focus on relevant source words instead of compressing an entire sentence into a single fixed-size bottleneck vector.
2017 "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al.) Introduced the Transformer, completely replacing recurrence with self-attention and enabling massive parallelisation across sequences.
2018 BERT (Google) & GPT-1 (OpenAI) Established the pretrain-then-fine-tune paradigm using bidirectional encoders (BERT for language understanding) and causal decoders (GPT for generation).
2019 GPT-2, T5 & DistilBERT Demonstrated zero-shot scaling (GPT-2), unified all NLP tasks into text-to-text (T5), and proved knowledge distillation could shrink BERT by 40% while keeping 97% performance (DistilBERT).
2020–Present LLMs (GPT-3/4, LLaMA) & Vision Transformers (ViT) Scaled parameters to hundreds of billions for emergent reasoning and extended self-attention beyond text to images, audio, and biology (AlphaFold).

What RNN / LSTM problems did the Transformer solve? Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and LSTMs process tokens sequentially one step at a time ($t_1 \rightarrow t_2 \rightarrow \dots \rightarrow t_n$), which prevents parallel computation across a sequence and makes training on large datasets extremely slow. Furthermore, information from early tokens must travel through many recurrent steps, causing vanishing gradients and short-term memory bottlenecks on long sequences. Transformers solve both issues by using self-attention to connect any two tokens directly in $O(1)$ path length while processing every token in the sequence simultaneously.

1.3 Impact and Disadvantages of Transformers¶

Real-World Impact (Tasks Transformed):

  • Machine Translation: Fluent, context-aware translation across hundreds of languages (e.g., T5, NLLB).
  • Search & Information Retrieval: Semantic search engines that match user intent rather than exact keywords (e.g., BERT in Google Search).
  • Conversational AI & Chat Assistants: General-purpose reasoning, summarisation, and Q&A systems.
  • Code Completion & Software Engineering: Real-time code synthesis and debugging (e.g., GitHub Copilot, CodeLLaMA).
  • Computer Vision & Multimodal AI: Image classification, segmentation, and text-to-image generation via Vision Transformers (ViT, DiT).
  • Computational Biology: Predicting 3D protein structures directly from amino acid sequences (AlphaFold 2/3).

Key Disadvantages:

  • Quadratic Attention Cost ($O(N^2)$): Every token attends to every other token, causing compute and memory to grow quadratically with sequence length $N$.
  • Fixed Context Window: Models are restricted by a hard maximum token limit (e.g., 512 tokens in DistilBERT) determined during pretraining.
  • High Compute & Memory Footprint: Billions of parameters require substantial RAM/VRAM and energy for both training and inference.
  • Data Hunger: Pretraining from scratch requires massive corpora because Transformers lack the built-in sequential inductive bias of RNNs or CNNs.
  • Hallucinations: Generative decoders predict statistically plausible next tokens rather than verifying facts, often fabricating false information confidently.
  • Opaque Behaviour: Despite visualising attention weights, understanding exact multi-layer reasoning across millions of weights remains difficult.

=== Sub-word Splitting on Rare/Long Words ===
Raw Text      : antidisestablishmentarianism and hyperparameters
Sub-word Pieces: ['anti', '##dis', '##est', '##ab', '##lish', '##ment', '##arian', '##ism', 'and', 'hyper', '##para', '##meter', '##s']

Role of [CLS], [SEP], and Sub-word Tokenisation:

  • [CLS] (Classification Token, ID 101): Placed at the very beginning of every sequence. Its final-layer hidden state aggregates information from the entire sequence and is fed into the classification head for tasks like sentiment analysis.
  • [SEP] (Separator Token, ID 102): Marks the end of a sequence (or separates two distinct sentences in tasks like question answering and natural language inference).
  • Why Sub-words instead of Whole Words? Word-level vocabularies explode in size and fail completely on unseen or misspelled words ([UNK]), whereas character-level vocabularies produce sequences that are too long and lose word-level meaning. WordPiece sub-word tokenisation keeps common words intact (e.g., "understand") while breaking rare or complex words (like "hyperparameters" $\rightarrow$ ['hyper', '##para', '##meter', '##s']) into known root and suffix pieces (marked with ##), eliminating out-of-vocabulary errors with a compact 30,522-token vocabulary.

Why do we need Padding and an attention_mask? GPUs and PyTorch tensors require rectangular matrices where every row in a batch has the exact same length. To batch a 4-token sequence with a 15-token sequence, the shorter sequence is padded with [PAD] tokens (ID 0) up to length 15. The attention_mask assigns 1 to real tokens and 0 to [PAD] tokens, instructing the self-attention layers to assign zero weight to padding positions so dummy tokens do not corrupt the representation of short sentences.

Task 2: Self-Attention & Scaled Dot-Product Attention¶

  • Objective: Implement scaled dot-product self-attention and Luong dot attention from scratch in NumPy, demonstrate the necessity of $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling and positional information, and verify our mathematical implementation against DistilBERT's real Layer 0, Head 0 weights.
  • Expected Output: Intermediate Q/K/V shapes, a 4×4 self-attention heatmap (plots/attention_scratch.png) with row-sum verification, a scaling saturation experiment, Luong attention weights and comparison table, an order-blindness proof, and a zero-error np.allclose match against DistilBERT.

2.1 The Core Idea of Self-Attention¶

In self-attention, every input token embedding is projected by three learned weight matrices into three distinct vectors:

  • Query ($Q$ — "What am I looking for?"): Represents the current token's request for contextual information from other tokens in the sentence.
  • Key ($K$ — "What information do I offer?"): Acts like an index label describing what kind of information each token holds.
  • Value ($V$ — "What content do I pass on?"): Contains the actual semantic information contributed by a token once it is attended to.

To update a token's representation, we compute the dot product between its Query and every token's Key ($Q K^T$), scale and normalise those scores into probabilities using Softmax, and compute a weighted average of all Value vectors. Because these matrix multiplications happen across all tokens simultaneously, the entire sequence is processed in parallel, eliminating the slow step-by-step bottleneck of RNNs and LSTMs.

2.2 Scaled Dot-Product Attention from Scratch¶

In [20]:
np.random.seed(42)

def stable_softmax(z, axis=-1):
    """Numerically stable softmax by subtracting the row-wise maximum."""
    z_shifted = z - np.max(z, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    exp_z = np.exp(z_shifted)
    return exp_z / np.sum(exp_z, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
In [21]:
def scaled_dot_product_attention(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    d_k = Wk.shape[-1]
    Q = X @ Wq
    K = X @ Wk
    V = X @ Wv

    # Scaled dot-product scores
    scores = (Q @ K.T) / np.sqrt(d_k)
    weights = stable_softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    output = weights @ V
    return Q, K, V, scores, weights, output

2.3 Why Divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?¶

In [28]:
np.random.seed(42)

def compute_entropy(probs):
    """Compute Shannon entropy per row (in nats), averaged over rows."""
    eps = 1e-12
    return -np.sum(probs * np.log(probs + eps), axis=-1).mean()
In [29]:
records = []
n_tokens = 10

for d_k in [4, 256]:
    Q_sim = np.random.randn(n_tokens, d_k)
    K_sim = np.random.randn(n_tokens, d_k)
    raw_dot = Q_sim @ K_sim.T

    for scaled in [True, False]:
        s = raw_dot / np.sqrt(d_k) if scaled else raw_dot
        w = stable_softmax(s, axis=-1)

        max_prob = w.max(axis=-1).mean()
        avg_entropy = compute_entropy(w)
        score_std = s.std()

        records.append({
            "d_k": d_k,
            "Scaled (1/sqrt(d_k))": "Yes" if scaled else "No",
            "Score Std Dev": round(score_std, 3),
            "Avg Max Softmax Prob": round(max_prob, 4),
            "Avg Row Entropy": round(avg_entropy, 4)
        })
In [30]:
df_scaling = pd.DataFrame(records)
print("=== Scaling Experiment Results (10 Tokens) ===")
print(df_scaling.to_string(index=False))

=== Scaling Experiment Results (10 Tokens) ===
 d_k Scaled (1/sqrt(d_k))  Score Std Dev  Avg Max Softmax Prob  Avg Row Entropy
   4                  Yes          0.927                0.2862           1.9893
   4                   No          1.854                0.4853           1.4645
 256                  Yes          0.943                0.2747           1.9824
 256                   No         15.095                0.8643           0.3332

Why divide scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$? If the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent random variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, their dot product $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ has a mean of $0$ and a variance of $d_k$ (standard deviation $\sqrt{d_k}$). When $d_k$ is large (e.g., $d_k = 256$), unscaled dot products grow huge in magnitude ($\text{Std} \approx 16$), pushing the Softmax function into extreme saturation where the highest score receives a probability near 1.0 and all other tokens get nearly 0.0 (entropy collapses toward $0$). In this saturated region, Softmax gradients become vanishingly small during backpropagation, stalling learning; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance ($\text{Std} \approx 1$) regardless of head dimension.

2.4 Comparison: Luong Attention vs. Transformer Self-Attention¶

Feature Luong Attention (Seq2Seq RNN) Transformer Self-Attention
Where $Q, K, V$ Come From Query: Current decoder hidden state $s_t$.
Keys & Values: Same encoder hidden states $h_1, \dots, h_n$ (no separate $Q/K/V$ projections in pure dot form).		 Query, Key & Value: All three are projected via learned matrices ($W_Q, W_K, W_V$) from the same sequence of token representations.
What Is Attended Over One decoder step looks back across all source encoder states (cross-sequence alignment). Every token in a sequence looks at every other token within the same sequence ($N \times N$ all-to-all).
Needs an RNN? Yes — relies on an LSTM/GRU to build sequential hidden states before computing attention. No — completely replaces recurrence; acts as the primary feature extractor itself.
Parallelism Sequential across decoder steps ($t_1, t_2, \dots$) because $s_t$ depends on $s_{t-1}$. Fully parallel across all tokens in the sequence during training and encoding.
Where It Sits in Architecture A bridge module sitting between the recurrent encoder and recurrent decoder. The core building block stacked inside every layer of the encoder and decoder.

restored_output = output_from_shuffled[inv_perm]

print("Permutation indices               :", perm)
print("Shuffled output == Original[perm]? :", np.allclose(output_from_shuffled, expected_shuffled_output))
print("Restored output == Original output?:", np.allclose(restored_output, attn_output))
print("Max absolute difference           :", np.max(np.abs(restored_output - attn_output)))

Permutation indices               : [2, 0, 3, 1]
Shuffled output == Original[perm]? : True
Restored output == Original output?: True
Max absolute difference           : 1.7763568394002505e-15

Why is Self-Attention Order-Blind? Self-attention computes dot products and weighted sums across sets of vectors without any built-in recurrence or index awareness. As proven above, permuting the input rows simply permutes the output rows in the exact same way ($\text{Attention}(P X) = P \, \text{Attention}(X)$), meaning "The dog bit the man" and "The man bit the dog" produce identical token representations if word order is not injected. This permutation equivariance is the exact reason Task 3 introduces Positional Encoding to stamp each token with its position index before entering the attention layers.

What does a successful match prove? Matching DistilBERT's internal attentions[0][0, 0] tensor down to floating-point precision ($\sim 10^{-8}$ max difference) proves that a production Hugging Face Transformer executes the exact same mathematical equation we wrote from scratch in NumPy: $\text{Softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{64}}\right)$. There is no hidden magic inside the pretrained model—it simply projects the 768-dimensional embeddings via q_lin and k_lin, splits them into 12 parallel heads of size 64, scales the dot products by $\sqrt{64} = 8$, and normalises each row with Softmax (since model.eval() disables dropout).

Task 3: Multi-Head Attention, Positional Encoding & Layer Normalization¶

  • Objective: Inspect how Multi-Head Attention captures diverse linguistic patterns across heads, implement Sinusoidal Positional Encoding and Layer Normalization from scratch in NumPy, and compare them against DistilBERT's learned positional embeddings and Batch Normalization.
  • Expected Output: A 2×3 grid of real attention head heatmaps (plots/attention_heads.png), head entropy bar charts for early vs. late layers, a sinusoidal positional encoding heatmap (plots/positional_encoding.png), cosine similarity checks for word positions and DistilBERT's 512 learned embeddings, and a verified LayerNorm vs. BatchNorm comparison.

3.1 Why Multi-Head Attention Instead of One Single Head?¶

A single attention head can only focus on one dominant relationship per token at a time (because Softmax forces weights to sum to 1), which is insufficient when a word simultaneously has syntactic, semantic, and coreference links in a sentence. In Multi-Head Attention, the hidden dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ is split across $h$ parallel subspaces of size $d_k = d_{\text{model}} / h$ (in DistilBERT, $768 = 12 \text{ heads} \times 64 \text{ dimensions}$). Each head learns its own independent $W_Q^{(i)}, W_K^{(i)}, W_V^{(i)}$ projection matrices to capture a distinct linguistic pattern, and the resulting $h$ outputs are concatenated back into a $768$-dimensional vector and mixed through a final linear output projection $W_O$. Because each head operates on a reduced dimension $d_k = d_{\text{model}} / h$, the total floating-point computation and parameter count remain almost identical to using a single full-sized head of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$.

Distinct Attention Behaviours Observed Across Heads:

  1. Positional / Adjacent-Token Tracking (e.g., Layer 0, Head 3): A strong diagonal or off-diagonal stripe appears where every token attends almost exclusively to the immediately preceding or following token, building local n-gram phrase context.
  2. Special-Token Attention Sink (e.g., Layer 2, Head 5 & Layer 5, Head 2): Vertical bright bands form on the [CLS] and [SEP] columns, acting as a global pooling mechanism or a default "no-op" sink when a head's specific linguistic pattern is not triggered.
  3. Semantic / Coreference Linking (e.g., Layer 3–4 Heads): In middle-to-late layers, the pronoun row "it" distributes significant attention weight back toward subject nouns like "animal" and adjectives like "tired", resolving what "it" refers to in context.

3.3 Head Diversity Measurement¶

In [56]:
def head_entropies(layer_attn_tensor):
    """
    layer_attn_tensor: shape (1, n_heads, seq_len, seq_len)
    Returns array of shape (n_heads,) with mean row entropy per head.
    """
    probs = layer_attn_tensor[0].numpy()
    eps = 1e-12
    ent_per_token = -np.sum(probs * np.log(probs + eps), axis=-1)
    return ent_per_token.mean(axis=-1)

Do early and late layers behave differently? On this single sentence, Layer 0 shows wide diversity across heads—some heads have very low entropy (sharply focused on adjacent tokens) while others have high entropy (broadly averaging across the whole sentence)—whereas Layer 5 exhibits more uniformly moderate-to-low entropy as heads converge on specific summary tokens ([CLS]/[SEP]) and task-relevant words before classification. Because this measurement is taken on just one 14-token sentence, this pattern is an illustrative snapshot rather than a universal law across all datasets.

3.4 Sinusoidal Positional Encoding from Scratch¶

In [60]:
def sinusoidal_positional_encoding(max_pos=50, d_model=128):
    pe = np.zeros((max_pos, d_model))
    positions = np.arange(max_pos)[:, np.newaxis]
    div_term = 10000.0 ** (np.arange(0, d_model, 2) / d_model)

    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(positions / div_term)
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(positions / div_term)
    return pe
In [61]:

print("=== Sinusoidal Positional Encoding ===")

Why Sines and Cosines of Different Frequencies? Using geometric wavelengths from $2\pi$ up to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ acts like a continuous binary clock: low dimension indices oscillate rapidly to distinguish adjacent tokens, while high dimension indices oscillate slowly to distinguish tokens far apart, giving every position a unique signature vector without adding learnable parameters. Furthermore, because $\sin(\text{pos}+k)$ and $\cos(\text{pos}+k)$ can be written as a linear matrix transformation of $\sin(\text{pos})$ and $\cos(\text{pos})$ via trigonometric addition identities, attention heads can easily learn to attend by relative distance $k$ regardless of absolute position.

3.5 Position Makes Identical Words Different¶

In [63]:
np.random.seed(42)

def cosine_sim(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

word_embedding = np.random.randn(128)
In [64]:

vec_pos20_no_pe = word_embedding
sim_without_pe = cosine_sim(vec_pos3_no_pe, vec_pos20_no_pe)
In [65]:

vec_pos20_with_pe = word_embedding + PE[20]
sim_with_pe = cosine_sim(vec_pos3_with_pe, vec_pos20_with_pe)

print(f"Cosine Similarity WITHOUT Positional Encoding : {sim_without_pe:.6f}")

=== Identical Word at Position 3 vs. Position 20 ===
Cosine Similarity WITHOUT Positional Encoding : 1.000000
Cosine Similarity WITH Positional Encoding    : 0.859478

How Adding Positional Encoding Removes Order-Blindness: Without positional encoding, two occurrences of the same word (e.g., "bank" at position 3 and "bank" at position 20) have identical vectors (cosine similarity $= 1.0$), which is why permuting rows in Task 2.5 left the self-attention weights unchanged. By adding PE[3] and PE[20] directly to the word embedding before Layer 0, the two instances become distinct vectors in representation space (cosine similarity drops to $\approx 0.65$), breaking permutation equivariance so Query-Key dot products now depend on both word identity and word order.

Learned Positional Embeddings vs. Sinusoids and Relative Biases: Instead of fixed mathematical sinusoids, BERT and DistilBERT learn a lookup table of position vectors (shape: 512 × 768) end-to-end during pretraining; the bright diagonal band in the heatmap shows that the model naturally learns to make nearby positions similar and distant positions less similar. Because this table only has 512 rows, the model literally has no position vector for index 512 or higher, which is the direct origin of DistilBERT's hard 512-token context window limit. By contrast, encoder-decoder models like T5 (explored in Task 5) omit absolute position embeddings entirely and instead inject learned relative position biases directly into the attention score matrix based on the distance $i - j$ between tokens.

3.7 Layer Normalization from Scratch¶

In [70]:
np.random.seed(42)

def layer_norm_scratch(X, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    """
    Normalise each token vector independently across its feature dimension (axis=-1).
    X shape: (seq_len, d_model)
    """
    mean = np.mean(X, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    var = np.var(X, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    X_norm = (X - mean) / np.sqrt(var + eps)
    return gamma * X_norm + beta
In [71]:

gamma_np = np.ones(8, dtype=np.float32)
beta_np = np.zeros(8, dtype=np.float32)

Y_np = layer_norm_scratch(X_ln, gamma_np, beta_np, eps=1e-5)

=== DistilBERT Embeddings LayerNorm Parameters ===
Weight (gamma) shape: (768,) | First 5 values: [0.8445 0.7974 0.7331 0.7594 0.8013]
Bias   (beta)  shape: (768,) | First 5 values: [ 0.0443  0.0614  0.0692  0.0874 -0.0584]
Criterion Batch Normalization (PR 2 / CNNs) Layer Normalization (Transformers)
What Is Normalised Over Normalises each feature channel across the batch/token dimension ($\text{axis}=0$). Normalises each individual token vector across all its $d_{\text{model}}$ features ($\text{axis}=-1$).
Dependence on Batch Size High — struggles with small batches ($B=1$) and requires running mean/variance buffers at inference. Zero — computed per token on the fly; behaves identically at batch size 1 and during training/inference.
Variable-Length Sequences & Padding Breaks down — [PAD] tokens and differing sequence lengths pollute batch statistics across positions. Immune — each token is normalised strictly using its own 768 features, unaffected by padding in other positions.
Why Transformers Use LayerNorm Unsuitable for autoregressive generation and padded NLP batches. Stabilises residual stream activations across deep layers independently for every token step.

What are $\gamma$ (weight) and $\beta$ (bias) in DistilBERT's LayerNorm? In model.distilbert.embeddings.LayerNorm, $\gamma$ (weight, shape 768) is a learnable per-feature scale vector (initialised near 1) and $\beta$ (bias, shape 768) is a learnable per-feature shift vector (initialised near 0). They allow the network to undo or adjust the strict zero-mean, unit-variance constraint on any of the 768 dimensions if preserving specific activation magnitudes helps downstream layers.

Task 4: Transformer Encoder Architecture & Masked Self-Attention¶

  • Objective: Dissect the internal layer structure and parameter distribution of the DistilBERT encoder, demonstrate bidirectional context using masked language modelling, and contrast bidirectional encoder attention against causal (masked) decoder self-attention in NumPy and GPT-2.
  • Expected Output: Printed DistilBERT architecture and module mapping table, parameter distribution bar/pie charts, top-3 fill-mask predictions on 3 sentences, bidirectional vs. causal attention heatmaps (plots/causal_mask.png) with an upper-triangular zero check (np.triu), and a padding vs. causal mask comparison.

4.1 The Transformer Encoder Block Architecture¶

Input Token IDs
      │
      ▼
[ Token Embeddings (30522×768) + Positional Embeddings (512×768) ]
      │
      ▼
[ Embedding LayerNorm + Dropout ]
      │
      ▼
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  × 6 Stacked TransformerBlock Layers (DistilBERT)         │
│                                                           │
│  Input X ──► [ Multi-Head Self-Attention (12 heads) ]     │
│     │                        │                            │
│     └──────────► (+) ◄───────┘  (Residual Connection 1)   │
│                   │                                       │
│                   ▼                                       │
│         [ sa_layer_norm (768) ]                           │
│                   │                                       │
│     ┌─────────────┴──────────────────────────┐            │
│     │                                        ▼            │
│     │             [ FFN: lin1 (768→3072) + GELU + lin2 ]  │
│     │                                        │            │
│     └──────────► (+) ◄───────────────────────┘ (Res. 2)   │
│                   │                                       │
│                   ▼                                       │
│        [ output_layer_norm (768) ]                        │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.2 Print and Read the Real Encoder¶

In [77]:
print(model.distilbert)

DistilBertModel(
  (embeddings): Embeddings(
    (word_embeddings): Embedding(30522, 768, padding_idx=0)
    (position_embeddings): Embedding(512, 768)
    (LayerNorm): LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12, elementwise_affine=True)
    (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
  )
  (transformer): Transformer(
    (layer): ModuleList(
      (0-5): 6 x TransformerBlock(
        (attention): DistilBertSelfAttention(
          (q_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (k_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (v_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (out_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
        )
        (sa_layer_norm): LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12, elementwise_affine=True)
        (ffn): FFN(
          (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
          (lin1): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=3072, bias=True)
          (lin2): Linear(in_features=3072, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (activation): GELUActivation()
        )
        (output_layer_norm): LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12, elementwise_affine=True)
      )
    )
  )
)

4.2 DistilBERT Module Name Mapping Table¶

Architectural Component Exact PyTorch Module Path in model.distilbert Weight / Layer Dimensions
Token Embedding embeddings.word_embeddings Embedding(30522, 768, padding_idx=0)
Position Embedding embeddings.position_embeddings Embedding(512, 768)
Embedding LayerNorm embeddings.LayerNorm LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12)
Attention Projections ($Q, K, V, O$) transformer.layer[i].attention.{q_lin, k_lin, v_lin, out_lin} $4 \times \text{Linear}(\text{in}=768, \text{out}=768)$
Attention LayerNorm (Norm 1) transformer.layer[i].sa_layer_norm LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12)
FFN Expansion (lin1) transformer.layer[i].ffn.lin1 Linear(in_features=768, out_features=3072)
FFN Activation transformer.layer[i].ffn.activation GELUActivation() ($4\times$ intermediate expansion)
FFN Projection (lin2) transformer.layer[i].ffn.lin2 Linear(in_features=3072, out_features=768)
Output LayerNorm (Norm 2) transformer.layer[i].output_layer_norm LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12)

4.3 Where Do the Parameters Live?¶

In [78]:
param_groups = {
    "Embeddings": 0,
    "Self-Attention": 0,
    "Feed-Forward (FFN)": 0,
    "Layer Norms": 0,
    "Classification Head": 0
}
In [79]:
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    count = param.numel()
    if "LayerNorm" in name or "layer_norm" in name:
        param_groups["Layer Norms"] += count
    elif "embeddings" in name:
        param_groups["Embeddings"] += count
    elif "attention" in name:
        param_groups["Self-Attention"] += count
    elif "ffn" in name:
        param_groups["Feed-Forward (FFN)"] += count
    elif "pre_classifier" in name or "classifier" in name:
        param_groups["Classification Head"] += count

Which component holds the most parameters, and what does that tell us? Across the 6 Transformer layers, the Feed-Forward Networks (FFN) hold the largest share of backbone weights (28.32M parameters, or 42.3% of the entire model—twice as many as the 14.17M in all Self-Attention layers combined), followed closely by the Embeddings lookup table (23.84M, or 35.6%). While self-attention routes contextual information between tokens, recent mechanistic interpretability research shows that the massive $768 \rightarrow 3072 \rightarrow 768$ FFN matrices act as giant key-value memory banks where most of the model's factual and world knowledge is actually stored.

4.4 Use the Encoder: Fill-Mask¶

In [83]:
unmasker = pipeline("fill-mask", model="distilbert-base-uncased")
In [84]:
masked_sentences = [
    "The capital of France is [MASK].",
    "The patient was rushed to the [MASK] by the paramedics for emergency surgery.",
    "Because the battery died, my [MASK] turned off right in the middle of a phone call."
]
In [85]:
print("=== Fill-Mask Top-3 Predictions ===")
for sent in masked_sentences:
    print(f"\nSentence: {sent}")
    preds = unmasker(sent, top_k=3)
    for rank, p in enumerate(preds, 1):
        print(f"  Top {rank}: {p['token_str']:<12} | Score: {p['score']:.4f} | Filled: {p['sequence']}")

=== Fill-Mask Top-3 Predictions ===

Sentence: The capital of France is [MASK].
  Top 1: marseille    | Score: 0.1427 | Filled: the capital of france is marseille.
  Top 2: nantes       | Score: 0.0902 | Filled: the capital of france is nantes.
  Top 3: toulouse     | Score: 0.0881 | Filled: the capital of france is toulouse.

Sentence: The patient was rushed to the [MASK] by the paramedics for emergency surgery.
  Top 1: hospital     | Score: 0.9112 | Filled: the patient was rushed to the hospital by the paramedics for emergency surgery.
  Top 2: ambulance    | Score: 0.0290 | Filled: the patient was rushed to the ambulance by the paramedics for emergency surgery.
  Top 3: clinic       | Score: 0.0088 | Filled: the patient was rushed to the clinic by the paramedics for emergency surgery.

Sentence: Because the battery died, my [MASK] turned off right in the middle of a phone call.
  Top 1: phone        | Score: 0.5380 | Filled: because the battery died, my phone turned off right in the middle of a phone call.
  Top 2: alarm        | Score: 0.0602 | Filled: because the battery died, my alarm turned off right in the middle of a phone call.
  Top 3: laptop       | Score: 0.0432 | Filled: because the battery died, my laptop turned off right in the middle of a phone call.

How fill-mask Demonstrates Bidirectional Encoder Behaviour: In Sentence 2 ("The patient was rushed to the [MASK] by the paramedics for emergency surgery.") and Sentence 3 ("Because the battery died, my [MASK] turned off right in the middle of a phone call."), the crucial clues "paramedics / surgery" and "phone call" appear to the right (after) the [MASK] token. Because an encoder has no causal mask, the [MASK] position simultaneously attends to left-context tokens ("patient", "battery") and right-context tokens ("surgery", "phone call"), allowing it to predict "hospital" and "phone" with high confidence.

Why Bidirectional Attention is Illegal in Next-Word Prediction: In the heatmap above, substantial non-zero weights appear above the main diagonal (for instance, "doctor" at row 2 attends forward to "patient" at column 5 and "[SEP]" at column 7). If a generative language model trained to predict the next token $w_t$ from $w_1, \dots, w_{t-1}$ were allowed to attend above the diagonal, it could simply "peek" at the ground-truth future tokens during training and copy the answer without learning anything—which is why generative decoders require masked (causal) self-attention.

4.6 Masked (Causal) Self-Attention from Scratch¶

In [91]:
np.random.seed(42)

n_causal = 6
d_k_causal = 8
causal_tokens = ["Artificial", "intelligence", "will", "transform", "the", "world"]

X_c = np.random.randn(n_causal, d_k_causal)
Wq_c = np.random.randn(d_k_causal, d_k_causal)
Wk_c = np.random.randn(d_k_causal, d_k_causal)
In [92]:
Q_c = X_c @ Wq_c
K_c = X_c @ Wk_c
raw_scores_c = (Q_c @ K_c.T) / np.sqrt(d_k_causal)
In [93]:
causal_mask = np.triu(np.full((n_causal, n_causal), -np.inf), k=1)
In [94]:
masked_scores_c = raw_scores_c + causal_mask
causal_weights_scratch = stable_softmax(masked_scores_c, axis=-1)
In [95]:
print("=== Causal Self-Attention from Scratch (6×6) ===")
print("Causal Mask Matrix:\n", causal_mask)
print("\nRow sums after Softmax      :", np.round(causal_weights_scratch.sum(axis=-1), 6))
print("All rows sum to 1.0?        :", np.allclose(causal_weights_scratch.sum(axis=-1), 1.0))
print("Max value above diagonal    :", np.triu(causal_weights_scratch, k=1).max())

=== Causal Self-Attention from Scratch (6×6) ===
Causal Mask Matrix:
 [[  0. -inf -inf -inf -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0. -inf -inf -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0. -inf -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0.   0. -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0.   0.   0. -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.]]

Row sums after Softmax      : [1. 1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]
All rows sum to 1.0?        : True
Max value above diagonal    : 0.0
In [96]:
plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
sns.heatmap(
    causal_weights_scratch, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="Oranges",
    xticklabels=causal_tokens, yticklabels=causal_tokens, cbar_kws={"label": "Attention Weight"}
)
plt.title("4.6 Masked (Causal) Self-Attention from Scratch (Lower-Triangular)")
plt.xlabel("Key Tokens (Past & Present Only)")
plt.ylabel("Query Tokens")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Why Add $-\infty$ Before Softmax Instead of Zeroing Weights Afterwards? Because $\exp(-\infty) = 0$, adding $-\infty$ to upper-triangular future positions before Softmax ensures two things simultaneously: future tokens receive exactly 0.0 probability, and the remaining valid past/present tokens in that row are properly normalised so their weights still sum to 1.0. If we instead ran Softmax over all tokens first and simply zeroed out the upper triangle afterwards, the remaining weights in each row would sum to less than 1.0 (failing to form a valid probability distribution) and the magnitudes of future tokens would still leak into the Softmax denominator $\sum_j \exp(s_{ij})$!

Feature Padding Mask Causal (Look-Ahead) Mask
Core Purpose Prevents real tokens from attending to dummy [PAD] tokens added only to make batch sequences equal length. Prevents a token at position $t$ from peeking at future tokens at positions $t+1, \dots, N$ during autoregressive generation.
Shape & Matrix Pattern Vertical zero columns on the right side of the attention matrix corresponding to wherever attention_mask == 0 (varies per sentence in a batch). Strict lower-triangular matrix (every entry above the main diagonal $j > i$ is masked out with $-\infty$ before Softmax, fixed for all sentences).
Which Model Families Use It All families when processing padded batches (Encoder-only, Decoder-only, and Encoder-Decoder). Decoder-only (e.g., GPT-2, LLaMA) and the Decoder self-attention stack of Encoder-Decoder models (e.g., T5, BART).

Task 5: Cross-Attention, Decoder Architecture & Autoregressive Inference¶

  • Objective: Understand encoder-decoder and decoder-only architectures, implement cross-attention extraction using t5-small, write a manual autoregressive generation loop, benchmark decoding strategies and KV-cache acceleration with GPT-2, and compare the three Transformer model families.
  • Expected Output: Translation and summarization outputs with t5-small, a cross-attention heatmap (plots/cross_attention.png) aligning output tokens to source tokens, a verified manual greedy decoding loop identical to model.generate(), a comparison table of 5 decoding strategies, KV-cache speed-up metrics, and a model family summary table.

5.1 The Transformer Decoder Block & Model Families¶

Target Input Tokens ──► [ Token Embeddings + Positional Encodings ]
                              │
                              ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  × N Stacked Decoder Blocks                                 │
│                                                             │
│  Input ──► [ Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention ]             │
│                 │                                           │
│                 └──────────► (+) ◄────────── (Res. + Norm)  │
│                               │                             │
│                               ▼                             │
│            [ Cross-Attention over Encoder Output ]          │
│                 │                         │                 │
│                 │ (Queries)               │ (Keys & Values) │
│                 └──────────► (+) ◄────────┘ (Res. + Norm)  │
│                               │                             │
│                               ▼                             │
│            [ Position-Wise Feed-Forward Network ]           │
│                 │                                           │
│                 └──────────► (+) ◄────────── (Res. + Norm)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
            [ Linear Projection + Softmax over Vocabulary ]

5.2 How Cross-Attention Works¶

In cross-attention, the three projection inputs come from two different sources:

  • Queries ($Q$) come from the DECODER's current hidden states (representing what the model is trying to write next).
  • Keys ($K$) and Values ($V$) come from the ENCODER's final output sequence (representing the source text).

This allows the decoder to dynamically look back across the entire source sentence at every generation step—serving the exact same conceptual role as Luong attention in recurrent seq2seq models (Task 2.4), but computed fully in parallel across all query tokens.

5.3 Run an Encoder-Decoder Model¶

In [110]:
from transformers import T5ForConditionalGeneration, T5Tokenizer
In [111]:
t5_pipeline_tok = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained("t5-small")
t5_pipeline_model = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("t5-small")
t5_pipeline_model.eval()
Out[111]:
T5ForConditionalGeneration(
  (shared): Embedding(32128, 512)
  (encoder): T5Stack(
    (embed_tokens): Embedding(32128, 512)
    (block): ModuleList(
      (0): T5Block(
        (layer): ModuleList(
          (0): T5LayerSelfAttention(
            (SelfAttention): T5Attention(
              (q): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=512, bias=False)
              (k): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=512, bias=False)
              (v): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=512, bias=False)
              (o): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=512, bias=False)
              (relative_attention_bias): Embedding(32, 8)
            )
            (layer_norm): T5LayerNorm()
            (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
          )
          (1): T5LayerFF(
            (DenseReluDense): T5DenseActDense(
              (wi): Linear(in_features=512, out_features=2048, bias=False)

Alignment Analysis in Cross-Attention: The heatmap reveals clear linguistic alignment: target decoder tokens attend strongly to their corresponding source words in the encoder input (e.g., "maison" attending heavily to "house", and "petite" attending to "small"), demonstrating how cross-attention bridges the source and target sequences during translation.

5.5 Inference is Autoregressive — Manual Loop¶

In [127]:
prompt = "Artificial intelligence will"
inputs_gen = gpt2_tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
input_ids = inputs_gen["input_ids"]
In [128]:
max_new_tokens = 20
In [130]:
manual_ids = input_ids.clone()
for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = gpt2_model(manual_ids)
        next_token_logits = outputs.logits[:, -1, :]  # Logits for the final token
        next_token = torch.argmax(next_token_logits, dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        manual_ids = torch.cat([manual_ids, next_token], dim=-1)

manual_text = gpt2_tok.decode(manual_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
In [131]:
with torch.no_grad():
    generated_ids = gpt2_model.generate(input_ids, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=False)
auto_text = gpt2_tok.decode(generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

print("=== Autoregressive Manual Decoding Loop ===")
print(f"Manual Generated Text : {manual_text}")
print(f"Model.generate() Text : {auto_text}")
print(f"Outputs are identical?: {torch.equal(manual_ids, generated_ids)}")

=== Autoregressive Manual Decoding Loop ===
Manual Generated Text : Artificial intelligence will be able to do things like search for and find people, and to do things like find out who
Model.generate() Text : Artificial intelligence will be able to do things like search for and find people, and to do things like find out who
Outputs are identical?: True

Why is Decoder Inference Autoregressive? Unlike encoders that process all tokens simultaneously in parallel, a decoder generates text one token at a time: at each step $t$, the model predicts the probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token based on the prompt and all previously generated tokens, appends the highest-scoring token (argmax), and feeds the expanded sequence back as input for step $t+1$.

5.7 KV-Cache Speed-Up¶

In [140]:
import time
In [141]:
kv_prompt = "Machine learning algorithms can analyze vast amounts of data to"
kv_inputs = gpt2_tok(kv_prompt, return_tensors="pt")
n_tokens_gen = 50
In [142]:
_ = gpt2_model.generate(**kv_inputs, max_new_tokens=10, use_cache=True)
In [143]:
times_true = []
for _ in range(3):
    start = time.time()
    _ = gpt2_model.generate(**kv_inputs, max_new_tokens=n_tokens_gen, use_cache=True)
    times_true.append(time.time() - start)
avg_time_true = np.mean(times_true)
In [144]:
times_false = []
for _ in range(3):
    start = time.time()
    _ = gpt2_model.generate(**kv_inputs, max_new_tokens=n_tokens_gen, use_cache=False)
    times_false.append(time.time() - start)
avg_time_false = np.mean(times_false)
In [145]:
speedup = avg_time_false / avg_time_true

print("=== KV-Cache Speed-Up Benchmark (50 New Tokens) ===")
print(f"Avg Time WITH KV-Cache    : {avg_time_true:.4f} seconds")
print(f"Avg Time WITHOUT KV-Cache : {avg_time_false:.4f} seconds")
print(f"Speed-Up Factor           : {speedup:.2f}x faster")

=== KV-Cache Speed-Up Benchmark (50 New Tokens) ===
Avg Time WITH KV-Cache    : 3.0855 seconds
Avg Time WITHOUT KV-Cache : 9.3680 seconds
Speed-Up Factor           : 3.04x faster

How the KV-Cache Accelerates Autoregressive Inference: Without a KV-cache, generating step $t$ requires recomputing Key and Value vectors for all $1, \dots, t-1$ previous tokens from scratch, resulting in $O(N^2)$ computational complexity over $N$ steps. With use_cache=True, the model caches previously computed Key and Value matrices in memory and only computes $K$ and $V$ for the single newly generated token at each step, reducing time complexity per step to $O(1)$ and yielding substantial speed-ups ($\approx 3\times$ to $5\times$ or higher).

5.8 Summary Table: The Three Transformer Model Families¶

Model Family Primary Attention Type(s) Used Can Generate Text? Position Embedding Scheme Typical Real-World Tasks Example Model Used in Notebook
Encoder-Only Bidirectional Self-Attention (Unmasked) No (outputs embeddings or logits per token) Learned Absolute Embeddings (BERT-style) Sentiment analysis, token classification, semantic search distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english
Decoder-Only Causal (Masked) Self-Attention Yes (autoregressive generation) Learned Absolute Embeddings / RoPE Text completion, chat assistants, code synthesis gpt2
Encoder-Decoder Bidirectional Encoder Self-Attention + Decoder Cross-Attention Yes (autoregressive generation from source) Relative Position Biases Machine translation, summarization, text-to-text transformation t5-small

6.3 Cost Grows with Sequence Length¶

In [169]:
lengths = [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]
pass_times = []
In [170]:
base_text = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog and explores the deep neural network architecture. "
In [171]:
for length in lengths:
    # Construct input of approx target token length
    constructed_text = (base_text * 20)[:length * 5]
    inputs_len = tok(constructed_text, truncation=True, max_length=length, return_tensors="pt")

    # Warm-up run
    with torch.no_grad():
        _ = model(**inputs_len)

    # Average of 10 runs
    latencies = []
    for _ in range(10):
        start_t = time.time()
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = model(**inputs_len)
        latencies.append(time.time() - start_t)

    pass_times.append(np.mean(latencies) * 1000)  # Convert to milliseconds

Observed Quadratic Cost vs. Sequence Length: Because self-attention computes an $N \times N$ attention score matrix for every head and layer, doubling the sequence length quadruples the number of attention operations, resulting in the characteristic non-linear latency curve measured above. This $O(N^2)$ computational explosion is the primary bottleneck driving fixed context windows (such as DistilBERT's 512 limit) and motivating sparse or linear attention variants in modern architectures.

6.5 Build the Mini Application¶

In [177]:
def text_toolkit(text):
    """
    Returns a dictionary with:
      (a) sentiment label and score (DistilBERT)
      (b) short summary (t5-small, max_length=60)
      (c) French translation of the summary (t5-small)
    """
    if not isinstance(text, str) or not text.strip():
        return {
            "Input Text": text,
            "Sentiment": "Error: Empty Input",
            "Score": 0.0,
            "Summary": "Error: Empty Input",
            "French Translation": "Error: Empty Input"
        }

    # Handle long input by truncating for pipeline safety
    clean_text = text.strip()

    # (a) Sentiment Analysis
    sent_res = clf(clean_text, truncation=True, max_length=512)[0]
    sentiment_label = sent_res["label"]
    sentiment_score = round(sent_res["score"], 4)

    # (b) Summarisation using t5-small
    sum_input = f"summarize: {clean_text}"
    sum_ids = t5_pipeline_tok(sum_input, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=512).input_ids
    with torch.no_grad():
        sum_out = t5_pipeline_model.generate(sum_ids, max_new_tokens=60, min_new_tokens=10, do_sample=False)
    summary_text = t5_pipeline_tok.decode(sum_out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

    # (c) French Translation of summary
    trans_input = f"translate English to French: {summary_text}"
    trans_ids = t5_pipeline_tok(trans_input, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=512).input_ids
    with torch.no_grad():
        trans_out = t5_pipeline_model.generate(trans_ids, max_new_tokens=60, do_sample=False)
    french_text = t5_pipeline_tok.decode(trans_out[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

    return {
        "Input Text": (clean_text[:60] + "...") if len(clean_text) > 60 else clean_text,
        "Sentiment": sentiment_label,
        "Score": sentiment_score,
        "Summary": summary_text,
        "French Translation": french_text
    }

6.6 Reflection — What I Learned About Transformers¶

  • (a) Best Understood vs. Unclear Concepts: I now have a solid understanding of how $Q, K, V$ projections drive scaled dot-product attention and how causal masks prevent future token leakage. The internal nuances of multi-head tensor reshaping and KV-cache memory management are still areas I want to explore more deeply through hands-on optimization.
  • (b) Theory vs. Reality: Recomputing Layer 0, Head 0 attention manually in NumPy and matching it to DistilBERT's weights down to $10^{-8}$ precision was satisfying because it proved there is no hidden magic—just clean linear algebra and Softmax. Being surprised by how much parameter weight resides in the FFN key-value memory banks rather than attention matrices was another great insight.
  • (c) Observed Disadvantages: Measuring the quadratic time growth ($O(N^2)$) with sequence length and observing how context truncation past 512 tokens leads to lost information quantified the exact trade-offs of Transformer architectures in practice.
  • (d) Real-World Application: I would build an automated multi-lingual customer support ticket classifier and summarizer using an encoder-decoder framework (such as T5 or BART) to ingest customer complaints, categorise sentiment, and generate concise multi-lingual case summaries for support teams.
